full_judgment:
Md Mizanur Rahman Bhuiyan J : This request of the accused-petitioners, eleven (11) in number, namely, 1. Abdul Halim Gazi, 2. Bappi Gazi, 3. Halim Talukder, 4. Jakir Talukder, 5. Kabir Talukder, 6. Azmir Hossain Talukder, 7. Akkas Sikder, 8. Tipu Sultan, 9. Joyanto Kumar Saha, 10. Touhid alias Thohidul Anowar and 11. Zahid Hossain Talukder focused on section 498 of The Code of Criminal Procedure (for short The Code) knocking the door of this Court is the second journey craving for anticipatory bail in Special Tribunal Case No. 7 of 2004 arising out of Jhalakati Police Station Case No. 9 dated 6-3-2004 under section 4 of The Explosive Substance Act, 1908 now pending before Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati. 

 8. Meaning and definition of bail stated in the foregoing paragraphs indicate that there is not much of difference between "bail" and "anticipatory bail". The only distinction between "bail" and "anticipatory bail" is that where as the former is granted after arrest, and, therefore, means release from custody and the latter is granted in anticipation of arrest and the power is exercisable in case of an anticipated accusation of an offence and is effective at the very moment of arrest. 

 9. The Code originally did not contain any specific provision for anticipatory bail. By Ordinance XLIX of 1978 provision of anticipatory bail has been provided on insertion of section 497A in The Code. The inserted section 497A postulated that when any person had reason to believe that he might be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he might apply to the High Court Division or the Court of Session or the Sub-divisional Magistrate for a direction under this section; and that Court or the Magistrate might, if it or he thought fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, he would be released on bail. Section 497A empowered the High Court Division or the Court of Session or the Sub-divisional Magistrate to include such conditions in the directions under sub-section (1) in the light of the fact of the particular case as it might think fit. But by Ordinance No.IX of 1982, the provision of anticipatory bail engrafted in section 497A by Ordinance No. XLIX of 1978 stood omitted. 

 11. In Muhammad Ayub vs Md Yakub, 19 DLR (SC) 38 it has been held: Section 498 would be called in aid before the Court of Sessions and the High Court even where the Court is not seized directly of the proceeding in question and where no actual arrest has been made so far but anticipatory bail is asked for e.g. where the case is still at a stage of investigation by the police or pending in a Subordinate Court. 

 Generally speaking, the main circumstance as would entitle an order for extraordinary remedy of pre-arrest bail is the perception of the Court upon the facts and materials disclosed by the petitioner before it that the Criminal proceeding which is being or has been launched against him is being or has been taken with an ulterior motive, political or otherwise, for harassing the accused and not for securing justice, in a particular case. 

 The only other case where the prayer may also be considered may occur if it is proved that on account of some local public commotion or other circumstances it is not possible for the petitioner to appear before the lower Court for seeking bail. The petitioner must, however, remain physically present in Court before his application for bail can be entertained. 

 Ordinarily, when a person is wanted in connection with a non-bailable offence of grave nature he is not entitled to anticipatory bail. All persons charged with non-bailable offences must be treated equally unless, of course, there are special circumstances which need special consideration in the particular facts of a case. 

 Anticipatory bail should be granted by the High Court Division for a limited period or till filing of the charge-sheet, whichever is appropriate in the circumstances of the case. After expiry of the period of filing of the charge-sheet, as the case may be, the accused must appear before the Court concerned and obtain fresh bail from the Court on the merit of the case. 

 Granting of anticipatory bail in an exceptional circumstance is a matter to be decided by the learned Judges on the facts of a particular case. The special and exceptional circumstances are to be left to the discretion of the learned Judges." 

 Ordinarily, this Court is loath to interfere with the orders granting or refusing bail but it cannot be an insurmountable obstacle in the way of rectifying an order which tends to disclose miscarriage of justice. 

 16. In Patwary Rafiquddin Haider vs State and another, 7 BLC 432 (to which one of us AK Badrul Huq, J was a party), law on anticipatory bail and authorities on anticipatory bail of the Apex Courts of The Sub-continent such as Muhammad Ayub vs Md Yakub (Supra), State vs Abdul Wahab Shah Chowdhury and another (Supra), Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia vs State of Punjab (Supra), Pokar Ram vs State of Rajasthan (Supra) and Salahuddin Abdul Samad Shaikh vs State of Maharashtra (Supra) have been taken stock of and the submission of learned Counsels and fact and circumstances of the case had been, also, considered and anticipatory bail to the accused-petitioner till submission of Police Report or on completion of investigation had been granted and there was an order to the effect that in the event of submission of charge-sheet the accused- petitioner was to surrender to the regular Court i.e. the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong and the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate was directed to consider bail matter on materials placed before him and, also, in consonance with laws and principles regulating grant or refusal of bail and the petition for anticipatory bail stood disposed of. 

 17. The scope of granting anticipatory bail after submission of charge-sheet came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of India in Bharat Chaudhary and another vs State of Bihar and another, 2003 SCC (Criminal) 1953. An application for anticipatory bail by husband and wife who were accused by their daughter-in-law of offences punishable under sections 504, 498A and 406 of The Penal Code and sections 3/4 of The Dowry Prohibition Act was rejected by the High Court of Judicature at Patna and the order of rejection of anticipatory bail was under challenge before the Supreme Court in a Criminal Appeal. Contention was raised from the respondent State that since the Court of first instance had taken cognizance of the offence in question, section 438 of The Code of Criminal Procedure could not be used for granting anticipatory bail even by that Court and the only remedy available to the appellants was to approach the trial Court and surrender and thereafter apply for regular bail under section 439 of The Code of Criminal Procedure. The case of Salauddin Abdul Samad Shaikh vs State of Maharashtra, (1996) 1 SCC 667 = 1996 SCC (Cri) 198 had been relied upon in support of the contention. The Supreme Court of India on perusal of section 438 of The Code of Criminal Procedure found no restriction in regard to the exercise of power of granting anticipatory bail in a suitable case either by the Court of Session, High Court or Supreme Court even when cognizance is taken or a charge-sheet had been filed. Supreme Court held: 

 "The object of section 438 of The Code is to prevent undue harassment of the accused persons by pre-trial arrest and detention. The fact, that a Court has either taken cognizance of the complaint or the investigating agency has filed a charge-sheet, would not by itself, in our opinion, prevent the concerned Courts from granting anticipatory bail in appropriate cases. The gravity of the offence is an important factor to be taken into consideration while granting such anticipatory bail so also the need for custodial interrogation, but these are only factors that must be borne in mind by the concerned Courts while entertaining a petition for grant of anticipatory bail and the fact of taking cognizance or filing of charge-sheet cannot by themselves be construed as a prohibition against the grant of anticipatory bail. In our opinion, the Courts i.e. the Court of Sessions, High Court or this Court has the necessary power vested in them to grant anticipatory bail in non-bailable offences under section 438 of The Code of Criminal Procedure even when cognizance is taken or charge-sheet is filed provided the facts of the case require the Court to do so". 

 The Supreme Court in laying down the above principle considered the earlier case Salauddin Abdul Samad Shaikh vs State of Maharashtra (Supra). 

 18. The Supreme Court of India in above Bharat Chaudhary and another vs State of Bihar and another (Supra) though laid down that anticipatory bail can be granted after submission of charge, the same cannot bind us in view of the law and principles propounded by our Appellate Division in respect of granting anticipatory bail in State vs Abdul Wahab Shah Chowdhury and another (Supra) which is an authority of our Jurisdiction wherein it has been stated that anticipatory bail should be granted by the High Court Division for a limited period or the filing of charge-sheet, whichever is appropriate in the circumstances of the case and after expiry of the period of filing of charge-sheet, as the case may be, the accused must appear before the Court concerned and obtain fresh bail from the Court on the merit of the case. The law and principle settled in the above authority is binding upon this Court on the strength of Article 111 of The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 19. The conspectus which emerges from the above authorities of Apex Courts is that anticipatory bail is an extraordinary remedy which can be granted only in exceptional and extraordinary circumstances upon a proper and intelligent exercise of discretion and upon facts and materials disclosed by the petitioner seeking anticipatory bail before Court in a Criminal Proceeding which is being launched or has been launched against him with ulterior motive, political or otherwise, for causing harassment and humiliation to accused person and not for ends of justice. Anticipatory bail must be for a limited period/duration or till submission of Police Report in the form of charge-sheet and that will be dependent upon the facts and circumstances of each and every case. Anticipatory bail, thus, cannot be granted in all cases as a matter of course and has to be granted only in exceptional cases. The Court when approached for anticipatory bail is to consider whether in the facts and circumstances of the case judicial discretion should be exercised in favour of the person seeking anticipatory bail and the discretion to be exercised must be informed by tradition, methodised by analogy and disciplined by system. 

 C. One Dalim, a supporter of Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) nominated candidate Mr Mahbub Hossain, died on 10-30 AM on the spot as a result of bomb explosion at the time of preparing bomb and nobody was responsible for the death. Following bomb explosion First Information Report was lodged with Jhalakati Police Station leading to Jhalakati Police Station Case No. 9 dated 6-5-2004 and three persons including petitioner Nos. 6 and 11 had been named in First Information Report. 

 d. Accused-petitioners in anticipation of arrest in Jhalakati Police Station Case No. 9 dated 6-5-2004 on 22-5-2004 on surrender before another Division Bench of The High Court Division sought anticipatory bail and High Court Division by order dated 22-5-2004 was pleased to enlarge the accused-petitioners on bail for a period of three months or till submission of Police Report whichever was earlier. 

 f. On the basis of a Protest (Naraji) Petition laid by learned Public Prosecutor, the case was transmitted to Police for holding further investigation on 13-6- 2004 and after a perfunctory investigation police on 21-7-2004 submitted charge-sheet against fifteen (15) accused person including the petitioner No.1 and other petitioners who are supporters of petitioner No.1 and who actively worked for the petitioner No.1 in the Pourashava election. Supplementary charge-sheet had been laid at the instance of the Hon'ble State Minister Mr Shahjahan Omar. 

 II. Since the case has been lodged under Explosive Substance Act, Courts below might not grant bail to accused-petitioners and, as such, this Hon'ble Court may graciously be pleased to grant anticipatory bail to accused-petitioners. 

 23. In State vs MA Malik (Supra) High Court Division granted anticipatory bail to the accused who stood indicted by his wife for offence punishable under section 6 of The Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 after submission of charge-sheet. It was contended from the State in Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 108 of 1994 that the High Court Division committed error of law in granting anticipatory bail to the respondent (accused) after submission of charge-sheet. Their Lordships of Appellate Division held that the spouses were at loggerhead and both of them having taken recourse to Court and there was possibility of the respondent being harassed in the circumstances stated by him in his petition and it was difficult to hold that the High Court Division exercised its discretion unreasonably or unfairly. Judgment of the cited case had been dated September 4, 1994. Judgment in State vs Abdul Wahab Shah Chowdhury had been pronounced on May 25, 1999 and it is later in point of time. Fact and circumstances of the cited case is quite distinguishable in the fact and circumstances of the case in hand inasmuch as the cited case is not a case of second journey of anticipatory bail as of present case and factual matrix is, also, different. It is well to remember that each and every judgment is to be made applicable in the fact and circumstances of each and every case. 

 25. Faced with factual scenario and circumstances of the case as well as legal predicament in seeking anticipatory bail for second time, learned Counsel for accused-petitioners candidly submitted that he is not pressing for anticipatory bail and accused-petitioners are willing to surrender before Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati and they may be afforded an opportunity to surrender before Special Tribunal No. 1 within a reasonable time so that they can seek bail before Special Tribunal No. 1 and a direction may be, also, recorded by this Court to the police authority not to apprehend them within the period granted by this Court for their surrender and appearance before Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati. 

 28. On glancing over the petition for anticipatory bail, examination of grounds pressed into service and giving an eye over facts and circumstances of the case, we are of this considered and dispassionate view that a direction may be recorded to the accused-petitioners in the matter of their surrender before Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati within a period fixed by this Court enabling them to seek bail there and in the interest of justice a direction may be, also, given to the Police authority not to apprehend the accused-petitioners within the period fixed by this Court. In Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 6604 of 2001, Colonel (Retired) Shawkat Ali and others vs State, Colonel (Retired) Shawkat Ali was granted anticipatory bail for a period of three months or till submission of Police Report whichever was earlier. In the said case charge-sheet had been submitted against the accused Colonel (Retired) Shawkat Ali. Accused Colonel (Retired) Shawkat Ali was directed to appear before Regular Court i.e. Court of Magistrate, and to seek bail before the Court. The Judgment is dated June 26, 2002 and one of us (AK Badrul Huq, J.) was a party to the Judgment. 

 29. Accused-petitioners, eleven (11) in number, namely, 1. Abdul Halim Gazi, 2. Bappi Gazi, 3. Halim Talukder, 4. fakir Talukder, 5. Kabir Talukder, 6. Azmir Hossain Talukder, 7. Akkas Sikder, 8. Tipu Sultan, 9. Joyanto Kumar Saha, 10. Touhid alias Thohidul Anowar and 11. Zahid Hossain Talukder are thus directed to surrender before Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati which is, also, Court of Sessions Judge, Jhalakati within a period of four (4) weeks from date. Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati shall consider bail of the accused-petitioners upon materials placed before it and in consideration of the fact and circumstances of the case and, also, in consonance with laws and principles regulating grant or refusal of bail. Discretion to be exercised by Special Tribunal No. 1, Jhalakati in grant or refusal of bail is to be informed by tradition, methodised by analogy, disciplined by system and sub-ordinated to the primordial necessity of order in social life. The police authority is, also, directed not to apprehend the accused-petitioners within the period of four (4) weeks from date.
